newsitem.title: BULGARIA: World Bank warns Bulgaria of further bank failures.
newsitem.headline: World Bank warns Bulgaria of further bank failures.

text.p: The World Bank warned that Bulgaria's plans for a fixed exchange rate regime to stabilise the lev will not solve the problems of illiquid banks and more failures could follow.

"Unless Bulgarian commercial banks are stablised by the time the currency board is introduced, they face a new crisis," World Bank resident representative Alberto Musalem told a seminar on Bulgaria's economic prospects.
"If interest rates do not fall, banks' portfolios will be seriously disbalanced," he added.
Local bank portfolios are plagued by three-digit interest rates and billion-lev non-performing loans.
World Bank economist Lyubomir Hristov told the seminar, which ended late on Monday, the currency board could fail if the banking crisis was not resolved before its implementation.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposed the implementation of a currency board last year to restore confidence in the ailing financial system.
The mechanism requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank.
Political deadlock created by the refusal of the ruling Socialists to agree to opposition calls for early elections has delayed talks on measures to haul the country out of its economic crisis.
Closing down insolvent banks to restructure the financial sector was part of reform agreements with the World Bank and the IMF, which the ex-communist ruling party failed to meet.
The central bank has sought insolvency for 15 local banks since May 31 but there has been no final court ruling on any of them so far.
"The legal system must speed up its bankruptcy procedures. It is absurd for a court to delay ruling on an insolvency case for nine months," said Hristov.
Hristov warned the delay would cause further erosion of confidence in the banking system.

Some $1 billion was withdrawn from commercial banks last year as panicked depositors rushed to convert savings into dollars. Further $1.5 billion are kept outside banks by the population as matress money, unofficial estimates show.
The lev hit a new historic low of 1,020 per dollar on Monday from around 600 at the beginning of the year and near 70 a year ago.
A second wave of massive deposit withdrawal was looming as Bulgaria's economy plunged into hyper-inflation, local bankers said.
Inflation for the first 15 days of January hit 30.8 percent and economists expected monthly inflation at 50 percent.
Foreign investors attending the seminar, which discussed Bulgarian economic prospects, said improvement of macro-economic indicators would boost investors' confidence in Bulgaria.
